en: The Scripture on the Buddha’s Teaching on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in the Warm Chamber, translated by the Anxi Tripitaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Ānanda said: "I have heard this from the Buddha: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha."

In the city of Rājagṛha, within the Śiśumāragiri mountains, there was a great elder’s son named Jīvaka, who was a great king of physicians. He treated all manner of illnesses; from his youth he had been fond of learning, and his talents and skills were exceptionally proficient.

He possessed deep understanding of the Five Classics, astronomy, and geography. Among those he treated, there were none whom he did not cure; the dead were restored to life, and funeral carriages were turned back.
His virtues were so numerous that they could not be fully recounted;
the eight kingdoms revered him, and all who saw him were filled with joy.
Thereupon, Jīvaka suddenly conceived a thought in the night:
"Tomorrow, when I reach the Buddha's dwelling, I shall ask him about my doubts.
At dawn, he commanded all his family members, both great and small, to prepare themselves and proceed to the Buddha's dwelling.
Upon arriving at the gate of the vihāra, he beheld the Buddha resplendent, his light illuminating heaven and earth.
The fourfold assembly sat in attendance, numbering many millions; the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they listened with single-minded tranquility.
Jīvaka and his retinue alighted from their carriage and proceeded directly forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and each sat to one side.
The Buddha consoled him, saying:
"Welcome, King of Physicians!
I wish to ask you something; do not hesitate or feel any difficulty."
Jīvaka knelt upright and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have been born into this world, I am coarse and uncultivated by nature; I have followed the common tide of worldly customs and have never performed meritorious deeds."
I now wish to invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks, as well as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, to enter the warm bathhouse for a cleansing bath.
I pray that all sentient beings may attain purity throughout the long night, that their defilements and impurities be eliminated, and that they encounter no further afflictions.
"Only by the Buddha’s holy will shall my aspiration not be disregarded!
The Buddha said to the King of Physicians,
"Excellent, O Wondrous Intention!"
He treated the illnesses of the multitude, and all received healing; those far and near relied upon his blessings, and there were none who did not rejoice.

Now he has again invited the Buddha and the assembly of monks to enter the warm bathhouse for a wash. May this merit extend to the multitudes of the ten directions who take medicine to treat their ailments; through bathing, may their defilements be removed, and their blessings shall be immeasurable.
"Listen attentively with a single mind; I shall first explain for you the merit of bathing the assembly of monks and the rewards thereof!
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"The method of bathing requires seven items to eliminate seven ailments and obtain seven kinds of meritorious retribution."
What are the seven items? First, fire;
second, pure water.
Third, soap powder;
fourth, ghee and oil;
fifth, concentrated lye.
Sixth, a tooth-stick;
seventh, an undergarment.
These are the methods for bathing.
What is meant by the removal of the seven ailments?
First, the four great elements are at peace;
second, the ailment of wind is eliminated.
Third, it removes dampness and rheumatism;
fourth, it removes cold and ice;
fifth, it removes heat and vapor.
Sixth, the removal of impurities;
seventh, physical agility and clarity of vision.
These constitute the removal of the seven ailments of the Saṃgha.
By making such offerings, one obtains seven blessings.
What are the seven blessings?
First, the four great elements will be free from disease; wherever one is born, one will always be at peace; one will be brave, martial, and robust, and be revered by all.
Second, his birth is pure; his countenance is upright and handsome, and neither dust nor water adheres to him;
he is revered by all people. Third, his body is constantly fragrant and his clothing is pristine; those who see him rejoice, and there are none who do not pay him respectful homage.
Fourth, his flesh and body are supple and lustrous, and his majestic radiance and virtue are so great that all revere and praise him; he walks alone without equal.
Fifth, they will have many followers who sweep away dust and grime; they will naturally receive blessings and always remember their past lives.
Sixth, their mouths and teeth will be fragrant and beautiful, square, white, and even; all those to whom they give instructions or commands will receive them with solemnity and obedience.
Seventh, in whatever place they are born, they will naturally possess clothing, ornaments, and precious jewels, such that all who see them will be moved to awe and reverence.
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"Performing this bathing ceremony for the assembly of monks and bodhisattvas brings these seven merits:
by reason of these causes and conditions, one may become a minister;..."
Some become emperors;
some become the sun, the moon, or the Four Heavenly Kings;
some become Śakra or a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King.
Some are reborn in the Brahma Heaven, where they receive immeasurable blessings;
others become Bodhisattvas, resolving their minds to uphold the stages [of the path], until their merit is perfected and their will fulfilled, ultimately attaining Buddhahood.
"By this causal connection, making offerings to the Sangha—the immeasurable field of merit—neither drought nor flood can cause harm.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse for the sake of Jīvaka:
"Observe within the three realms, Where devas and humans receive great blessings; The merit-field of the Saṃgha is supreme, A field that yields abundant fruit."
Virtue is boundless; listen attentively as I explain it next.
When a person lives in this world, they are upright and respected by others, and their nature remains ever pure;
this is due to having bathed in the waters of the Sangha.
If one becomes the son of a great minister, wealth and status shall always be peaceful and auspicious;
being brave, robust, and virtuous among the wise, one will move in and out without hindrance.
What one says will be respectfully adopted by others, and one’s body shall always be fragrant and pure.
An upright appearance and composed demeanor result from washing the Saṃgha.
If one is born into the family of a heavenly king, one is naturally pure upon birth;
one bathes with fragrant water and perfumes the body with incense.
His physical form differs from that of others; all who behold him are filled with joy.
This was created for bathing in a warm chamber—the meritorious reward for washing the Sangha.
First among the Four Heavenly Kings, he presides over the four quarters of the realm.
The body of radiant light is upright and handsome; its majestic virtue protects the four quarters.
The sun, moon, and constellations shed their brilliance to dispel the darkness;
this results from having washed the Saṃgha, for the retribution of merit follows like a shadow or an echo.
In the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Lord of Śakra is named Indra;
his precious city has six tiers, and his palaces are made of the seven treasures.
He is the courageous and honored one among the gods, upright in form and long-lived.
This arises from washing the assembly of monks; its retribution is beyond compare.
Like a Wheel-Turning King of the world, with the seven treasures leading the way before him, he travels throughout the four seas, accompanied by eighty-four thousand troops and horses.
Bright jewels illuminate day and night; Jade maidens provide offerings according to the season.
Their upright bodies are fragrant and pure— This results from having washed the assembly of monks.
In the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Contentment, One is uniquely honored within the realm of desire.
The celestial lord’s radiance is sufficient, his majestic spirit shakes the six heavens;
naturally partaking of ambrosia, with celestial maidens always by his side,
his manifold virtues are difficult to praise— this is due to having washed the assembly of monks.
The Brahmā, Māra, and Śubhakṛtsna devas dwell in the Pure Abodes, practicing spontaneously;
their conduct is pure and free from defilement, and they are devoid of female forms.
Cultivating the pure Brahma-faring, they purify themselves and set their will firmly upon Nirvāṇa.
To be born among those gods is due to having washed the assembly of monks.
The Buddha is the Honored One of the three realms;
he practiced the Way with extreme hardship and diligence, accumulating merit through countless eons, and has now attained true enlightenment.
A golden body with necklaces of jade, Dust and grime do not cling to the person;
The marks and signs are fully perfected— This results from washing the assembly of monks.
All Buddhas attain [enlightenment] through practice; Various [merits] are gained without toil or exertion.
To those beings within the three realms, there is nowhere his giving does not reach;
the Sangha is the holy and venerable one, the excellent field of merit for the four paths.
From within this, virtue and the Way emerge; this practice is the most wondrous truth.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he addressed Jīvaka once more:

“Observe those within the three realms—the various classes of humans and devas, their high or low status, their long or short lifespans, and the extent of their merit—all arise from the inequality of their mental applications in previous lives; therefore, what they receive differs, being as diverse as this.
That they receive such various rewards of fortune is solely because they have bathed the holy assembly!”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named?
By what means should it be used for exhortation?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is entitled 'The Sutra on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in a Warm Chamber.
It was spoken by all Buddhas; it was not created by me alone."
"The practitioner attains deliverance; it is not bestowed by a deity.
Seeking pure merit, one should personally practice accordingly.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Jīvaka and his retinue rejoiced upon hearing the teaching and all attained the stage of Srotāpanna. They prostrated before the Buddha and requested leave, preparing the implements for bathing.
The assembly, both great and small, each attained the stage of the Path; they all bowed their heads together in prostration, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
[Thus ends] the *Buddhabhāṣita-jentāka-snāna-bhikṣu-saṃgha-sūtra*.
